title: 5% Rates, Bessent's Failed Gamble & What Comes Next w/ Krishna Guha | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 78

metadata.title: 5% Rates, Bessent's Failed Gamble & What Comes Next w/ Krishna Guha | The Real Eisman Playbook Ep 78

summary: Krishna Guha explains the new Fed regime, the September hike, rising long yields and the distinction between firm forward commitments and useful policy communication. He links AI investment and fiscal borrowing to rates while separating AI capex from housing sensitivity. Eisman repeats his QE skepticism and concludes Treasury buybacks failed. The official record supports the policy shifts and buyback scale, while the strongest causal claims about QE, credibility and yield suppression require counterfactual analysis.
assessment: Claims are assessed individually. Empirical premises are not treated as successful forecasts. Unverified magnitudes and causal stories remain unresolved; subjective investment judgments are not assigned directional wins.
speaker_map_notes: Steve Eisman interviews Krishna Guha. Guha supplies most policy analysis; Eisman explicitly states QE skepticism, an exploratory liquidity-regulation theory and the closing buyback-failure judgment.
framework_points: Separate short policy rates, neutral rates and long-term risk premia.
Separate stock and flow, liquidity support and yield control.
Different sectors have different financing sensitivities.
tools_and_charts: FOMC decisions, speeches and balance-sheet task-force output.
Ten-year yields, issuance by maturity, term-premium estimates and buyback results.
PCE, labor-market data, AI capex and wealth-sensitive consumption.
transcript_cautions: Auto-captions repeatedly render Warsh as Walsh and misspell names.
The phrase 40 trillion deficit refers in context to a debt stock or Treasury-market scale, not an annual deficit; do not score it as a separate thesis.
Guha's expectations are not automatically Eisman forecasts.
Closing recap merges repetitions; advertisements excluded.

claims.claim: The September rate increase aimed to prevent persistent above-target inflation from becoming embedded in wages, pricing and expectations.
claims.speaker: Krishna Guha

claims.reason: The FOMC's explanation supports the inflation-risk rationale. This is contemporaneous policy interpretation, not a forecast.

evidence.finding: The FOMC unanimously raised its target range 25 basis points to 3.75%-4%, citing elevated inflation, resilient spending and robust investment.

claims.reason: Direction is clear but no date or disinflation threshold is specified; the short elapsed period cannot settle the durable inflation claim.

claims.claim: Treasury is effectively stepping into QE or Operation Twist by issuing short-term paper to buy long-term bonds.
claims.speaker: Steve Eisman
claims.test: Reconcile Treasury financing and maturity composition separately from Federal Reserve asset purchases.
claims.reason: Debt-financed repurchases can change maturity supply but do not create central-bank reserves like QE. Official program purposes are liquidity and cash management; the exact marginal funding mix requires issuance evidence.

evidence.title: FAQs about Treasury Securities Buybacks
evidence.finding: Liquidity-support buybacks target off-the-run liquidity, while cash-management operations manage seasonal cash and bill issuance. Treasury says the program is not intended to mitigate acute market stress.

claims.next_check: Reconcile Treasury financing and maturity composition separately from Federal Reserve asset purchases.

claims.reason: The program size and liquidity purpose are verified. Yield suppression, trader psychology and backing off are causal or intent claims not established by those documents.
